layout.description: A miniature circuit breaker has two trip units: a bimetal strip that bends slowly on overload, and a coil that opens at once on a short circuit. We show both on their own time scale, as a time-lapse and in slow motion.
layout.companion_text: Schematic model of a miniature circuit breaker after a BBC patent (1986), not a specific product. Time-lapse and slow motion refer to the limits in the standard (1.45 times the rated current: trip within 1 h; characteristic B from 5 times the rated current: under 0.1 s). The course of the trip curve between these points is schematic. Work on electrical installations belongs in the hands of a qualified electrician.

beats.spoken: On overload it takes its time, on a short circuit it doesn't. This small switch holds two trip units, each with its own clock.
This is a miniature circuit breaker. It protects the cable in the wall. Under the housing sit a bimetal strip, a coil, a latch, the contacts and the arc plates.

First, overload. If too many devices hang on one circuit, more current flows than the cable can carry for long. The bimetal warms up and bends, very slowly. At 1.13 times the rated current, the standard says the breaker must not trip for an hour; at 1.45 times, it must trip within an hour.

Then the short circuit. The current jumps to many times its value. The bimetal is too slow for that; now the coil opens the contact with its magnetic field. With characteristic B, this must happen in under a tenth of a second from five times the rated current. The arc runs into the arc plates.

The trip curve shows both: at the top the slow bimetal, at the bottom the steep step of the coil. With characteristic C the step sits higher, at five to ten times, for devices with high inrush current.
Two trip units, two time scales, one lever. And work on the installation belongs in the hands of a qualified electrician.
